analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA block imports of food linked to repeated contamination outbreaks.
analysis.headline: The Imported Food Safety Improvement Act of 2009 never got a vote: after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on June 10, 2009, it moved to a Health subcommittee and died there with no further action and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given the Health and Human Services Secretary new power to refuse entry to imported food — or all food of a certain type from a country, region, producer, or shipper — when that food has been repeatedly tied to foodborne illness outbreaks or found adulterated, poses a serious health risk, and is likely to be contaminated again. It also allowed emergency bans after a single outbreak causing serious illness or death, with a process for exporters to seek reversal once they clean up their act. It required that any ban stay consistent with U.S. trade agreements, and it never received a hearing, a vote, or a cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers who eat imported food would gain protection from imports repeatedly linked to foodborne illness. The bill gave health officials a targeted tool to cut off repeat offenders — a specific country, grower, factory, or shipper — rather than case-by-case shipments, and required the ban to be lifted once the source took remedial action.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary could refuse admission to food from any country, growing area, producer, manufacturer, or shipper whose food has been associated with repeated separate outbreaks of foodborne disease or repeatedly found adulterated, presents a reasonable probability of causing significant adverse health consequences or death, and is likely to cause disease or be adulterated again without systemic changes.

The Secretary could make an emergency determination to refuse admission to food strongly associated with a single outbreak that caused serious adverse health consequences or death, effective immediately for at least 30 days.

The bill included a built-in path back: an affected country, producer, or shipper could submit a rescission request with supporting evidence, and the Secretary had to act within 90 days or the food would be readmitted.
Any refusal of admission had to be carried out in a manner consistent with bilateral, regional, and multilateral trade agreements, which limited the reach of the new power.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign food producers, growers, manufacturers, and shippers whose products have been repeatedly linked to contamination would bear the cost of losing access to the U.S. market until they fixed their processes, and food importers and retailers who rely on those sources would face supply disruptions. Taxpayers would fund the new FDA regulatory work, which the bill required to be finalized within 90 days of enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Repeat-offense foreign food exporters and importers

drawbacks.text: The bill required any import ban to be consistent with U.S. trade agreement obligations, which could invite trade disputes or constrain how aggressively the Secretary acted against a country's food.
If the Secretary failed to act on a rescission request within 90 days, the refused food would automatically become admissible again, creating a risk that a deserved ban could lapse through inaction.

A ban on an entire type of food from an entire country based on repeat problems could impose broad costs on compliant producers and raise prices or limit choices for consumers, even though the bill allowed remediation-based reversals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a faster, broader tool to keep repeat-contamination food out of the country — is real and modest in scope, aimed only at sources with repeated outbreaks or adulteration findings and a high probability of causing serious harm. The main costs fall on the foreign producers and importers responsible, plus some administrative burden; the trade-agreement constraint and the 90-day auto-admission rule temper the bill but don't undercut its purpose. A reasonable, if narrow, food safety measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on June 10, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and that was the last action of any kind on the bill.
No member cosponsored the bill at any point during the two-year Congress.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any consideration in the Senate before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign food exporters with repeated contamination records and the importers who rely on them are better off, since no new authority to block their products was ever created. American consumers gained nothing, but nothing was lost either, since the bill was too small to matter much either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign food exporters and their importers

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Imported Food Safety Improvement Act of 2009 in the House.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Henry Waxman (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, passed it to its Health subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so support and opposition were never measured — it simply died in committee with a lone Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Foreign food producers, manufacturers, and shippers
industries.note: The bill would let the government cut off market access for any of them whose food is repeatedly linked to outbreaks or adulteration, with a 90-day path to reversal after remediation. Their gain from the bill's death is that repeat-offense sources kept selling into the U.S. market.

Importers and grocers relying on foreign suppliers would have faced sudden supply gaps when a source was banned. They also benefit, like all consumers, from safer imports, so their stake cuts both ways.
